storyboard.title: The Silk Road: Connecting East and West

scenes.heading: The Silk Road: Connecting East and West
scenes.subheading: A vast network stitches continents together
scenes.narration: For over a thousand years, a vast network of routes stitched continents together across Eurasia.
It began around 130 BC when China's Han Dynasty sent envoys westward seeking allies against the Xiongnu. Zhang Qian's diplomatic mission marked the true beginning of the Silk Road.
These land paths stretched over 6,400 kilometers, making it the longest land-based trade route in history.
Chinese silk traveled west to Europe, while Buddhism moved east from India to China and Central Asia.
Traders also carried major religions like Islam, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism across the steppes.
Papermaking technology spread from China through the Arab world and onward to Europe along these paths.
Under the Mongol Empire, 75 percent of the routes were unified, creating a rare peacetime for safe passage.
The Black Death in the 14th century disrupted travel along the routes, killing an estimated 25 million people.
By the 15th century, rising maritime routes and heavy Ottoman taxes made the land network less attractive.

checks.original: For over a thousand years, a vast network of routes stitched continents together across Eurasia.
It began around 130 BC when China's Han Dynasty sent envoys westward seeking allies against the Xiongnu.
Zhang Qian's diplomatic mission marked the true beginning of the Silk Road.
These land paths stretched over 6,400 kilometers, making it the longest land-based trade route in history.
Chinese silk traveled west to Europe, while Buddhism moved east from India to China and Central Asia.
Traders also carried major religions like Islam, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism across the steppes.
Papermaking technology spread from China through the Arab world and onward to Europe along these paths.
Under the Mongol Empire, 75 percent of the routes were unified, creating a rare peacetime for safe passage.
The Black Death in the 14th century disrupted travel along the routes, killing an estimated 25 million people.

The Silk Road connected East and West, exchanging goods, ideas, and culture for centuries before fading away.

facts.text: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century.
facts.quote: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century.

facts.text: The Silk Road spanned over 6,400 km (4,000 mi) on land.
facts.quote: Spanning over 6,400 km (4,000 mi) on land

facts.text: The Silk Road facilitated economic, cultural, political, and religious interactions between the Eastern and Western worlds.
facts.quote: it played a central role in facilitating economic, cultural, political, and religious interactions between the Eastern and Western worlds

facts.text: The name "Silk Road" was coined in the late 19th century.
facts.quote: The name "Silk Road" was coined in the late 19th century

facts.text: Historians prefer the term "Silk Routes" to describe the intricate web of land and sea routes connecting multiple regions.
facts.quote: some 20th- and 21st-century historians instead prefer the term Silk Routes, on the grounds that it more accurately describes the intricate web of land and sea routes

facts.text: The Silk Road was never a single east-west trade route linking China to the Mediterranean, nor was there unrestricted trade before the Mongol Empire.
facts.quote: Silk Road was never a singular east-west trade route that linked China to the Mediterranean, nor was there unrestricted trade before the Mongol Empire

facts.text: The Mongolian Empire controlled 75 percent of the Silk Road, unifying warring nations and creating peacetime.
facts.quote: During the Mongolian reign, 75 percent of the Silk Road fell under Mongolian control which served to unify the warring nations and bring about peacetime.

facts.text: The Silk Road existed for over 1,000 years, spanning the rise and fall of the Han Dynasty, Mongol Empire, Roman Empire, and the beginning of the British Empire.
facts.quote: The Silk Road spanned over 1,000 years outlasting empires, disease, wars, and famines. It saw the rise and fall of the Han Dynasty, the Mongol Empire and the Roman Empire, and even lasted until the beginning of the British Empire.

facts.text: The Silk Road built upon earlier Persian Empire courier routes from Susa to the Mediterranean Sea established between 500–330 BC.
facts.quote: the Silk Road actually built upon previously established routes forged during the Persian Empire between 500–330 BC

facts.text: The Han Dynasty initiated the Silk Road around 130 BC while seeking allies against the Xiongnu.
facts.quote: It was the Han Dynasty seeking allies in their war with the Xiongnu (the Huns), which would bring about The Silk Road.

facts.text: The Persian Royal Road had outposts with fresh horses so couriers could travel quickly from Susa to the Mediterranean Sea.
facts.quote: Along the route, outposts were established where fresh horses would be waiting so that couriers could travel quickly.

facts.text: The Bubonic Plague spread from Asia to Europe along the Silk Road via infected rats on trade caravans around 1346–1347 AD, killing an estimated 25 million people.
facts.quote: The Bubonic Plague started in Asia and China around 1346 AD. It spread along the Silk Road by infected rats accompanying the trade caravans. Within a year, the plague had reached Europe. It is estimated 25 million people died due to the plague.

facts.text: The Silk Road facilitated the exchange of goods, ideas, religions, and technologies between East and West.
facts.quote: The Silk Road facilitated the exchange of goods, ideas, religions, and technologies between East and West

facts.text: The Silk Road fostered cross-cultural interactions that enriched civilizations' knowledge in astronomy, medicine, and literature.
facts.quote: fostering cross-cultural interactions. It allowed for the spread of Buddhism to China, Chinese silk to Europe, and enriched both civilisations' knowledge in fields such as astronomy, medicine, and literature

facts.text: The Silk Road allowed the spread of Buddhism from India to China and Central Asia.
facts.quote: It allowed for the spread of Buddhism to China

facts.text: The Silk Road allowed Chinese silk to reach Europe.
facts.quote: Chinese silk to Europe

facts.text: Major religions such as Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Islam, and Christianity traveled along the Silk Road with traders.
facts.quote: Major religions like Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Islam, and Christianity travelled along with traders

facts.text: Papermaking technology spread from China to the Arab world and then to Europe via the Silk Road.
facts.quote: The Silk Road was vital in spreading papermaking technology from China to the Arab world, and eventually to Europe

facts.text: The Silk Road declined in the 15th century because maritime trade routes rose and the Ottoman Empire imposed restrictions.
facts.quote: The Silk Road's importance declined in the 15th century due to the rise of maritime trade routes and the Ottoman Empire's restrictions.

facts.text: The Ottoman Empire controlled key regions along the Silk Road and imposed heavy taxes and restrictions on trade.
facts.quote: The Ottomans, who controlled key regions along the Silk Road, imposed heavy taxes and restrictions on trade.

facts.text: Ottoman taxes and restrictions made the Silk Road less attractive, so merchants favored the new maritime routes.
facts.quote: This made the Silk Road less attractive for merchants, who began to favour the new maritime routes.

facts.text: Ottoman policies and the advantages of sea travel caused a significant decrease in trade volume on the Silk Road.
facts.quote: The Ottoman Empire's policies, coupled with the advantages of sea travel, led to a significant decrease in the volume of trade along the Silk Road.

facts.text: The Black Death in the 14th century had already disrupted Silk Road trade and caused a decline in its use.
facts.quote: the spread of the Black Death in the 14th century had already disrupted trade along the Silk Road, causing a decline in its use.

facts.text: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes connecting East and West that exchanged goods, ideas, and culture for centuries.
facts.quote: The Silk Road, a network of trade routes connecting East and West, was a vital artery for the exchange of goods, ideas, and culture for centuries.

facts.text: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes connecting Europe and Asia.
facts.quote: The Silk Road, a network of trade routes spanning Europe and Asia

facts.text: It operated from the 2nd century BC to the mid-15th century AD.
facts.quote: operated from the 2nd century BC to the mid-15th century AD

facts.text: The overland caravan routes covered between 6,400 and 10,000 kilometers.
facts.quote: the overland caravan routes covered between 6,400 and 10,000 kilometers

facts.text: The name 'Silk Road' comes from silk being a key export from China.
facts.quote: The route earned the name "Silk Road" because silk was a key export from China

facts.text: The term 'Silk Road' was first coined by German explorer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877.
facts.quote: The term "Silk Road" was first coined by German explorer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877

facts.text: The Silk Road was the longest land-based trade route in history.
facts.quote: The Silk Road was the longest land-based trade route in history

facts.text: Ferghana horses originated from the Ferghana Valley in modern-day Uzbekistan.
facts.quote: The Ferghana horses originated from the Ferghana Valley, a fertile region in modern-day Uzbekistan

facts.text: Ancient Chinese called Ferghana horses "heavenly horses."
facts.quote: often referred to as the "heavenly horses" by the ancient Chinese

facts.text: Emperor Wudi sent Zhang Qian on a diplomatic mission around 138 BCE.
facts.quote: Sent by Emperor Wudi around 138 BCE, Zhang Qian's journey marked the beginning of the Silk Road.

facts.text: Zhang Qian's journey marked the beginning of the Silk Road.
facts.quote: Zhang Qian's journey marked the beginning of the Silk Road.

facts.text: Zhang Qian was captured and detained by the Xiongnu for over a decade.
facts.quote: Despite being captured and detained by the Xiongnu for over a decade

facts.text: Ferghana horses significantly improved the mobility and effectiveness of Chinese military forces.
facts.quote: they significantly improved the mobility and effectiveness of Chinese military forces

facts.text: The Yam was a Mongol postal and messenger relay system.
facts.quote: was a Mongol postal system or supply point route messenger system

facts.text: Ögedei Khan expanded the Yam and gave it special attention because Mongol armies traveled quickly and their messengers had to be even faster.
facts.quote: Ögedei Khan gave special attention to the yam because Mongol armies traveled quickly; their messengers had to be even faster

facts.text: Messengers using the Yam covered 200–300 kilometres (120–190 mi) per day.
facts.quote: they covered 200–300 kilometres (120–190 mi) per day

facts.text: A messenger would hand off information to a fresh messenger at each station so documents kept moving without the rider getting tired.
facts.quote: A messenger would arrive at a station and give his information to another messenger, and meanwhile rest and let the other messenger go on to the next station to hand the document to yet another messenger

facts.text: The Secret History of the Mongols says Ögedei Khan founded the Yam, though a rudimentary system existed under Genghis Khan.
facts.quote: According to The Secret History of the Mongols, the yam was founded by Ögedei Khan. Other sources show that a rudimentary postal system had already existed during the reign of Genghis Khan.

facts.text: The Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople in 1453.
facts.quote: The capture of Constantinople (1453) to the Ottoman Turks was a key event.

facts.text: After capturing Constantinople, the Ottomans gained significant control of the Silk Road.
facts.quote: they now had significant control of the Silk Road, which European countries used to trade with Asia

facts.text: The claim that the Ottomans blocked the Silk Road by raising taxes lacks support from historical research.
facts.quote: this is not supported by any larger body of historical research

facts.text: There was no general decline in spice imports to Europe after 1453.
facts.quote: there was no general decline in spice imports to Europe after 1453

facts.text: Constantinople was not a major route for the spice trade.
facts.quote: Constantinople was not a major trade route in the spice trade

facts.text: Most spice trade came through Alexandria or Beirut instead of Constantinople.
facts.quote: most trade instead came from Alexandria or Beirut
